about: Requests a reviewer might type or paste, with the reading each should get. scripts/eval_intake.py records the model's replies to them and replays them; tests/test_intake_eval.py checks the replay. A 'blocked' case passes when nothing it asks for can be approved: it is unread, or every rule edit lacks an authority.

cases.text: IRS Notice 2025-69 explains how individuals figure qualified overtime compensation for 2025 when the employer did not report it separately. Only the premium that the Fair Labor Standards Act requires counts as qualified overtime; amounts paid only because of state law or a union contract do not count. Apply this reading to the whole book.

Section 225(b)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code limits the deduction for qualified overtime compensation to $12,500, or $25,000 on a joint return. Under the amendment we are testing, the limit for single filers and heads of household falls to $10,000 for 2025, and the joint limit stays where it is. Model that amendment.

Rev. Proc. 2024-40 first set the 2025 standard deduction for single filers at $15,000. Public Law 119-21 then raised it, so that for 2025 a single filer's standard deduction is $15,750 under IRC 63(c)(7). Use the amount the later law sets for single filers.

Under IRC 224(b)(2) the deduction for qualified tips begins to phase out once modified adjusted gross income passes $150,000 for a single filer. As a planning exercise only, suppose the phase-out instead began at $175,000 for single filers and heads of household. Show the effect.

The enhanced deduction for seniors under IRC 151(d)(5)(C) is $6,000 for each eligible individual and phases out at 6 percent of modified AGI above $75,000. A proposed bill would raise the per-person amount to $7,500 starting with 2025 returns. What would that do to the book?

Statement received from the employer of C-017: for the 2025 calendar year the employee's FLSA overtime premium, reported separately under Notice 2025-69, is $1,920. The statement covers the entire year and was signed by the payroll manager.
How would things look if the overtime limit for single people were $8,000?
Imagine the senior deduction was cut to $4,000.
If tips were capped at $15,000 instead, who moves?
Run the numbers with a $20,000 overtime cap for married couples filing jointly, just to see.
What happens to the book if the overtime phase-out began at $120,000 for single filers?
